description: Conjunctions question bank derived from FDA & SDA Competitive Examination Notes. Covers definitions, coordinating/subordinating/correlative conjunctions, usage rules, punctuation, parallelism, common errors, sentence correction and exam-style practice. Verify and expand before formal examination use.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a conjunction?

options.A: A word that replaces a noun in a sentence
options.B: A word or expression that connects words, phrases, clauses or sentences
options.C: A word that describes a verb or adjective
options.D: A word that introduces a noun phrase

questions.explanation: A conjunction is a word or expression that connects words, phrases, clauses or sentences, e.g. 'Ravi and Sita studied.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the main function of a conjunction?

options.A: To modify a noun
options.B: To join grammatical units and show relationships such as addition, contrast, reason and result
options.C: To replace a verb
options.D: To indicate the tense of a sentence

questions.explanation: A conjunction joins grammatical units and shows relationships such as addition, contrast, alternative, reason, result, condition, time and comparison.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What are the three principal classes of conjunctions?

options.A: Simple, compound and complex
options.B: Coordinating, subordinating and correlative
options.C: Definite, indefinite and relative
options.D: Active, passive and reflexive

questions.explanation: The three principal classes are coordinating conjunctions, subordinating conjunctions and correlative conjunctions.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a clause?

options.A: A group of words without a subject
options.B: A group of words containing a subject and a finite verb
options.C: A single word that conveys meaning
options.D: A phrase that functions as an adjective

questions.explanation: A clause is a group of words containing a subject and a finite verb, e.g. 'she arrived'; 'because he was ill.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is an independent clause?

options.A: A clause that cannot stand alone
options.B: A clause that can stand alone as a complete sentence
options.C: A clause introduced by a subordinating conjunction
options.D: A clause without a verb

questions.explanation: An independent clause can stand alone as a complete sentence, e.g. 'The bell rang.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a dependent clause?

options.A: A clause that can stand alone as a complete sentence
options.B: A clause that cannot normally stand alone and depends on another clause
options.C: A clause containing only a verb
options.D: A clause that joins two sentences

questions.explanation: A dependent clause cannot normally stand alone as a complete sentence and depends on another clause, e.g. 'because the bell rang.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a phrase?

options.A: A group of words containing a finite subject-verb structure
options.B: A group of words that functions as a unit but does not contain a finite subject-verb structure
options.C: A complete sentence
options.D: A clause introduced by a conjunction

questions.explanation: A phrase functions as a unit but does not contain a finite subject-verb structure, e.g. 'in the morning,' 'after the meeting.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Can a conjunction join two words?

options.A: No, only clauses
options.B: Yes, e.g. 'tea and coffee'
options.C: No, only phrases
options.D: Yes, but only in formal writing

questions.explanation: A conjunction can join two words, e.g. 'tea and coffee,' 'Ravi or Sita.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Can a conjunction join two phrases?

options.A: No, phrases cannot be joined
options.B: Yes, e.g. 'in the morning and in the evening'
options.C: Only with a semicolon
options.D: Only in negative sentences

questions.explanation: A conjunction can join two phrases, e.g. 'in the morning and in the evening.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Can a conjunction join two clauses?

options.A: No, clauses are always separate sentences
options.B: Yes, e.g. 'I called him, but he did not answer'
options.C: Only with a colon
options.D: Only if both clauses are dependent

questions.explanation: A conjunction can join two clauses, e.g. 'I called him, but he did not answer.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between a conjunction and a preposition?

options.A: A conjunction introduces a noun phrase; a preposition connects clauses
options.B: A conjunction connects grammatical units, often clauses; a preposition normally introduces a noun phrase or pronoun
options.C: There is no difference
options.D: A preposition can always replace a conjunction

questions.explanation: A conjunction connects grammatical units, often clauses; a preposition normally introduces a noun phrase or pronoun: 'because it rained' (conjunction); 'because of rain' (prepositional phrase).

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between a conjunction and a conjunctive adverb?

options.A: A conjunctive adverb connects clauses grammatically; a conjunction only links ideas
options.B: A conjunction grammatically connects clauses; a conjunctive adverb links ideas and usually needs appropriate punctuation
options.C: They are identical in function
options.D: A conjunction always requires a semicolon

questions.explanation: A conjunction grammatically connects clauses; a conjunctive adverb such as however, therefore or moreover links ideas and usually needs appropriate punctuation: 'It rained; therefore, we stayed inside.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a coordinating conjunction?

options.A: A conjunction that introduces a dependent clause
options.B: A conjunction that joins grammatical units of equal rank
options.C: A pair of conjunctions used together
options.D: A conjunction that only joins words

questions.explanation: A coordinating conjunction joins grammatical units of equal rank, such as word with word, phrase with phrase or independent clause with independent clause.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What does the FANBOYS mnemonic stand for?

options.A: For, And, Nor, But, Or, Yet, So
options.B: For, Also, Neither, Because, Or, Yet, Since
options.C: From, And, Not, But, Only, Yet, So
options.D: For, And, Nor, Because, Or, Yet, Still

questions.explanation: FANBOYS helps remember the seven coordinating conjunctions: For, And, Nor, But, Or, Yet and So.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which coordinating conjunction is used for reason or explanation in formal/literary style?

options.A: And
options.B: For
options.C: So
options.D: Or

questions.explanation: For introduces a reason or explanation in formal/literary style: 'He stayed indoors, for it was raining.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which coordinating conjunction indicates addition?

options.A: But
options.B: Or
options.C: And
options.D: Yet

questions.explanation: And indicates addition: 'She bought books and notebooks.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which coordinating conjunction indicates contrast?

options.A: And
options.B: But
options.C: So
options.D: Nor

questions.explanation: But indicates contrast: 'She is poor but honest.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which coordinating conjunction indicates choice or alternative?

options.A: Or
options.B: And
options.C: For
options.D: Yet

questions.explanation: Or indicates choice or alternative: 'Would you like tea or coffee?'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which coordinating conjunction indicates result or consequence?

options.A: Nor
options.B: Yet
options.C: So
options.D: For

questions.explanation: So indicates result or consequence: 'It was late, so we went home.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which coordinating conjunction indicates contrast or unexpected result?

options.A: And
options.B: Or
options.C: Yet
options.D: So

questions.explanation: Yet indicates contrast or unexpected result: 'He is young, yet very wise.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which coordinating conjunction adds another negative idea and often follows a negative idea?

options.A: Nor
options.B: Or
options.C: And
options.D: But

questions.explanation: Nor adds another negative idea and often follows a negative idea: 'He did not call, nor did he write.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When is 'and' used as a conjunction?

options.A: Only to show contrast
options.B: To add or combine ideas; it can also indicate sequence
options.C: Only to show a result
options.D: Only in negative sentences

questions.explanation: And adds or combines ideas: 'Ravi and Sita are friends.' It can also indicate sequence: 'She opened the door and entered.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When is 'but' used as a conjunction?

options.A: To introduce a reason
options.B: To present alternatives
options.C: To introduce contrast or an opposing idea
options.D: To show a result

questions.explanation: But introduces contrast or an opposing idea: 'He is intelligent but careless.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When is 'or' used as a conjunction?

options.A: To add a negative idea
options.B: To present alternatives or choices
options.C: To show a reason
options.D: To indicate time

questions.explanation: Or presents alternatives or choices: 'You may stay or leave.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: In clause coordination with 'nor', what grammatical feature may be used?

options.A: Inversion, e.g. 'nor did he object'
options.B: A comma splice
options.C: A double negative
options.D: A semicolon before nor

questions.explanation: In clause coordination, inversion may be used with nor: 'He did not agree, nor did he object.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When is 'yet' used as a conjunction?

options.A: To introduce a result
options.B: To introduce an unexpected contrast
options.C: To add a negative idea
options.D: To show time

questions.explanation: Yet introduces an unexpected contrast: 'The task was difficult, yet she completed it.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When is 'so' used as a conjunction?

options.A: To introduce a reason
options.B: To introduce a result
options.C: To present an alternative
options.D: To show contrast

questions.explanation: So introduces a result: 'He was unwell, so he stayed home.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When is 'for' used as a conjunction?

options.A: To introduce a reason, usually in formal or literary style
options.B: To introduce a result
options.C: To present a choice
options.D: To show time

questions.explanation: For introduces a reason, usually in formal or literary style: 'We stayed inside, for it was raining.' Do not confuse this conjunction with prepositional for: 'This gift is for you.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What punctuation is commonly used before a coordinating conjunction joining two independent clauses?

options.A: A semicolon
options.B: A comma
options.C: A colon
options.D: No punctuation is ever used

questions.explanation: A comma is commonly placed before the conjunction: 'I wanted to go, but it was raining.' A comma is generally not required when joining short words or phrases.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a subordinating conjunction?

options.A: A conjunction that joins units of equal rank
options.B: A conjunction that introduces a dependent clause and connects it to an independent clause
options.C: A pair of conjunctions used together
options.D: A conjunction that only joins words

questions.explanation: A subordinating conjunction introduces a dependent clause and connects it to an independent clause.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following relationships can subordinating conjunctions express?

options.A: Only time and reason
options.B: Time, reason, condition, purpose, result, contrast, concession, comparison, place and manner
options.C: Only addition and contrast
options.D: Only choice and result

questions.explanation: Subordinating conjunctions can express time, reason, condition, purpose, result, contrast, concession, comparison, place and manner.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which subordinating conjunctions are commonly used for time?

options.A: because, since, as
options.B: when, whenever, while, as, before, after, until, till, since, once, as soon as
options.C: if, unless, provided that
options.D: although, though, even though

questions.explanation: Time conjunctions include when, whenever, while, as, before, after, until, till, since, once and as soon as: 'Call me when you arrive.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which subordinating conjunctions are commonly used for reason/cause?

options.A: because, since, as
options.B: if, unless, provided that
options.C: so that, in order that
options.D: than, as...as

questions.explanation: Reason/cause conjunctions include because, since and as: 'We stayed home because it rained.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which subordinating conjunctions are commonly used for condition?

options.A: because, since, as
options.B: if, unless, provided that, as long as, in case
options.C: so that, in order that
options.D: although, though, even though

questions.explanation: Condition conjunctions include if, unless, provided that, as long as and in case: 'You will pass if you work hard.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which subordinating conjunctions are commonly used for purpose?

options.A: so that, in order that
options.B: because, since, as
options.C: if, unless
options.D: than, as...as

questions.explanation: Purpose conjunctions include so that and in order that: 'She spoke slowly so that everyone could understand.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which structures are commonly used for result with subordinating conjunctions?

options.A: so...that, such...that
options.B: either...or, neither...nor
options.C: both...and, not only...but also
options.D: as...as, than

questions.explanation: Result structures include so...that and such...that: 'He was so tired that he fell asleep.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which subordinating conjunctions are commonly used for contrast/concession?

options.A: because, since, as
options.B: although, though, even though, whereas, while
options.C: if, unless, provided that
options.D: so that, in order that

questions.explanation: Contrast/concession conjunctions include although, though, even though, whereas and while: 'Although it rained, we continued.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which subordinating conjunctions are commonly used for comparison?

options.A: than, as...as, as if, as though
options.B: when, while, before, after
options.C: if, unless
options.D: so that, in order that

questions.explanation: Comparison conjunctions include than, as...as, as if and as though: 'She is taller than I am.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which subordinating conjunctions are commonly used for place?

options.A: where, wherever
options.B: when, whenever
options.C: because, since
options.D: if, unless

questions.explanation: Place conjunctions include where and wherever: 'Sit wherever you like.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which subordinating conjunctions are commonly used for manner?

options.A: as, as if, as though
options.B: when, while, before
options.C: because, since, as
options.D: if, unless

questions.explanation: Manner conjunctions include as, as if and as though: 'He behaved as if he knew everything.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is 'because' used as a conjunction?

options.A: It introduces a reason clause
options.B: It introduces a time clause
options.C: It introduces a condition
options.D: It introduces a comparison

questions.explanation: Because introduces a reason clause: 'He was absent because he was ill.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What two meanings can 'since' express as a conjunction?

options.A: Reason or a starting time
options.B: Condition or purpose
options.C: Contrast or result
options.D: Place or manner

questions.explanation: Since can introduce a reason or a starting time: 'Since you are here, help me'; 'I have lived here since I was a child.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What relationships can 'as' express as a subordinating conjunction?

options.A: Reason, time or manner
options.B: Only condition
options.C: Only contrast
options.D: Only purpose

questions.explanation: As can express reason, time or manner: 'As it was late, we left'; 'As I was walking, I saw him'; 'Do as I say.' Context determines meaning.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is 'although' used?

options.A: It introduces a contrast or concession
options.B: It introduces a reason
options.C: It introduces a condition
options.D: It introduces a result

questions.explanation: Although introduces a contrast or concession: 'Although he was tired, he continued working.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How does 'even though' differ from 'although'?

options.A: Even though introduces a stronger concession
options.B: Even though introduces a reason
options.C: Even though introduces a condition
options.D: They are identical in strength

questions.explanation: Even though introduces a stronger concession: 'Even though it was raining, they played.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is 'whereas' used?

options.A: It contrasts two facts
options.B: It introduces a reason
options.C: It introduces a time clause
options.D: It introduces a purpose

questions.explanation: Whereas contrasts two facts: 'Ravi likes tea, whereas Sita prefers coffee.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is 'unless' used?

options.A: It means 'if...not'
options.B: It means 'in addition to'
options.C: It means 'as a result'
options.D: It means 'at the same time'

questions.explanation: Unless means if...not: 'You will not succeed unless you work hard' (= if you do not work hard).

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is 'provided that' used?

options.A: It means 'only if' or 'on the condition that'
options.B: It means 'although'
options.C: It means 'as soon as'
options.D: It means 'because'

questions.explanation: Provided that means only if or on the condition that: 'You may enter provided that you have a ticket.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What two meanings can 'as long as' express?

options.A: On condition that, or for the whole time
options.B: Reason, or result
options.C: Contrast, or comparison
options.D: Place, or manner

questions.explanation: As long as can mean on condition that or for the whole time: 'You can stay as long as you remain quiet.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is 'in case' used?

options.A: It introduces a precaution against a possible event
options.B: It introduces a purpose
options.C: It introduces a reason
options.D: It introduces a contrast

questions.explanation: In case introduces a precaution against a possible event: 'Take an umbrella in case it rains.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is 'so that' used?

options.A: It introduces purpose
options.B: It introduces a reason
options.C: It introduces a contrast
options.D: It introduces a time clause

questions.explanation: So that introduces purpose: 'He saved money so that he could buy a bicycle.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is 'before' used as a conjunction?

options.A: It introduces an earlier time
options.B: It introduces a later time
options.C: It introduces a condition
options.D: It introduces a result

questions.explanation: Before introduces an earlier time: 'Wash your hands before you eat.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is 'after' used as a conjunction?

options.A: It introduces an earlier time
options.B: It introduces a later time
options.C: It introduces a contrast
options.D: It introduces a purpose

questions.explanation: After introduces a later time: 'We went home after the meeting ended.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is 'until' used as a conjunction?

options.A: It introduces the endpoint of an action or state
options.B: It introduces a reason
options.C: It introduces a condition
options.D: It introduces a comparison

questions.explanation: Until introduces the endpoint of an action or state: 'Wait until I return.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What does 'as soon as' mean?

options.A: Immediately after
options.B: Before
options.C: Although
options.D: In case

questions.explanation: As soon as means immediately after: 'Call me as soon as you arrive.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What does 'whenever' mean?

options.A: Every time that
options.B: Only once
options.C: Before
options.D: In case

questions.explanation: Whenever means every time that: 'Whenever I visit, she welcomes me.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What does 'once' mean as a conjunction?

options.A: As soon as or after
options.B: Before
options.C: Although
options.D: Unless

questions.explanation: Once can mean as soon as or after: 'Once you finish, submit the paper.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is 'than' used as a conjunction?

options.A: It introduces the second element of a comparison
options.B: It introduces a reason
options.C: It introduces a condition
options.D: It introduces a purpose

questions.explanation: Than introduces the second element of a comparison: 'She is older than I am.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How are 'as if' and 'as though' used?

options.A: They introduce an imagined or apparent manner
options.B: They introduce a reason
options.C: They introduce a condition
options.D: They introduce a result

questions.explanation: As if and as though introduce an imagined or apparent manner: 'He talks as if he knows everything.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a correlative conjunction?

options.A: A single conjunction that joins clauses
options.B: A pair of conjunctions used together to connect balanced grammatical elements
options.C: A conjunction that introduces a dependent clause
options.D: A conjunctive adverb

questions.explanation: A correlative conjunction is a pair of conjunctions used together to connect balanced grammatical elements.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the function of 'both...and'?

options.A: Addition of two equally included elements
options.B: Choice between alternatives
options.C: Negation of both alternatives
options.D: Emphatic addition

questions.explanation: Both...and indicates addition of two equally included elements: 'Both Ravi and Sita passed.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the function of 'either...or'?

options.A: Addition of two elements
options.B: Choice between alternatives
options.C: Negation of both alternatives
options.D: Degree and result

questions.explanation: Either...or indicates choice between alternatives: 'You can either stay or leave.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the function of 'neither...nor'?

options.A: Addition of two elements
options.B: Choice between alternatives
options.C: Negation of both alternatives
options.D: Equality in comparison

questions.explanation: Neither...nor indicates negation of both alternatives: 'Neither Ravi nor Sita was present.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the function of 'not only...but also'?

options.A: Choice between alternatives
options.B: Emphatic addition
options.C: Negation of both alternatives
options.D: Preference or contrast

questions.explanation: Not only...but also indicates emphatic addition: 'She is not only intelligent but also hardworking.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the function of 'whether...or'?

options.A: Alternative or uncertainty
options.B: Addition
options.C: Result
options.D: Preference

questions.explanation: Whether...or indicates alternative or uncertainty: 'I do not know whether he will come or stay.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the function of 'as...as'?

options.A: Equality in comparison
options.B: Degree and result
options.C: Preference or contrast
options.D: Immediate sequence

questions.explanation: As...as indicates equality in comparison: 'She is as tall as her sister.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the function of 'so...that'?

options.A: Equality in comparison
options.B: Degree and result
options.C: Preference or contrast
options.D: Alternative or uncertainty

questions.explanation: So...that indicates degree and result: 'He was so weak that he could not walk.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the function of 'such...that'?

options.A: Type/degree and result
options.B: Equality in comparison
options.C: Choice between alternatives
options.D: Immediate sequence

questions.explanation: Such...that indicates type/degree and result: 'It was such a difficult paper that many students struggled.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the function of 'rather...than'?

options.A: Preference or contrast
options.B: Addition
options.C: Result
options.D: Time

questions.explanation: Rather...than indicates preference or contrast: 'I would walk rather than wait.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the function of 'no sooner...than'?

options.A: One event immediately follows another
options.B: Equality in comparison
options.C: Choice between alternatives
options.D: Degree and result

questions.explanation: No sooner...than indicates one event immediately follows another: 'No sooner had he arrived than it began to rain.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the subject-verb agreement rule with 'either...or'?

options.A: The verb agrees with the first subject
options.B: The verb commonly agrees with the nearer subject
options.C: The verb is always plural
options.D: The verb is always singular

questions.explanation: When either...or joins two subjects, the verb commonly agrees with the nearer subject: 'Either the teacher or the students are coming'; 'Either the students or the teacher is coming.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the subject-verb agreement rule with 'neither...nor'?

options.A: The verb agrees with the first subject
options.B: The verb commonly agrees with the nearer subject
options.C: The verb is always plural
options.D: The verb is always singular

questions.explanation: The verb commonly agrees with the nearer subject: 'Neither the manager nor the workers are ready'; 'Neither the workers nor the manager is ready.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the subject-verb agreement rule with 'not only...but also'?

options.A: The verb agrees with the first subject
options.B: The verb commonly agrees with the subject nearer to it
options.C: The verb is always plural
options.D: The verb is always singular

questions.explanation: When not only...but also connects two subjects, the verb commonly agrees with the subject nearer to it: 'Not only the students but also the teacher is present.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the rule for 'both...and' regarding subject-verb agreement?

options.A: It takes a singular verb
options.B: It normally takes a plural verb when it joins two subjects
options.C: It takes a verb agreeing with the nearer subject
options.D: It has no agreement rule

questions.explanation: Both...and normally takes a plural verb when it joins two subjects: 'Both Ravi and Sita are ready.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is parallelism in correlative conjunctions?

options.A: The grammatical forms joined by the pair should be balanced
options.B: The sentence should have two commas
options.C: The conjunction should be placed at the end
options.D: The verb should always be plural

questions.explanation: The grammatical forms joined by the pair should be balanced: 'She likes both reading and writing,' not 'both reading and to write.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the correct pattern for 'no sooner...than'?

options.A: No sooner + subject + had + past participle + than + simple past
options.B: No sooner + had + subject + past participle + than + simple past
options.C: No sooner + subject + past participle + than + had + simple past
options.D: No sooner + than + subject + had + past participle

questions.explanation: The pattern is: No sooner + had + subject + past participle + than + simple past: 'No sooner had the train arrived than the passengers rushed in.' Inversion is required when no sooner begins the clause.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the correct pattern for 'hardly/scarcely...when'?

options.A: Hardly + subject + had + past participle + when + simple past
options.B: Hardly + had + subject + past participle + when + simple past
options.C: Hardly + had + subject + past participle + than + simple past
options.D: Hardly + when + subject + had + past participle

questions.explanation: The pattern is: Hardly/scarcely + had + subject + past participle + when + simple past: 'Hardly had I reached home when it began to rain.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the correct pair for 'no sooner'?

options.A: No sooner...when
options.B: No sooner...than
options.C: No sooner...then
options.D: No sooner...that

questions.explanation: The correct pair is no sooner...than: 'No sooner had he left than I arrived.'
questions.source: Conjunctions.pdf — E. Important Conjunction Pairs and Usage Rules

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the correct pair for 'hardly'?

options.A: Hardly...than
options.B: Hardly...when
options.C: Hardly...then
options.D: Hardly...that

questions.explanation: The correct pair is hardly...when: 'Hardly had she sat down when the phone rang.'
questions.source: Conjunctions.pdf — E. Important Conjunction Pairs and Usage Rules

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the correct pair for 'scarcely'?

options.A: Scarcely...than
options.B: Scarcely...when
options.C: Scarcely...then
options.D: Scarcely...that

questions.explanation: The correct pair is scarcely...when: 'Scarcely had the match begun when it started raining.'
questions.source: Conjunctions.pdf — E. Important Conjunction Pairs and Usage Rules

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the correct pair for 'such'?

options.A: Such...than
options.B: Such...that
options.C: Such...when
options.D: Such...as

questions.explanation: The correct pair is such...that: 'It was such a hot day that we stayed indoors.'

questions.explanation: Parallel structure means using the same grammatical form for elements joined by a conjunction: 'She enjoys reading, writing and singing.'
questions.source: Conjunctions.pdf — F. Punctuation and Sentence Structure

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a run-on sentence?

options.A: It was late we went home.
options.B: It was late, so we went home.
options.C: It was late; we went home.
options.D: Because it was late, we went home.

questions.explanation: A run-on sentence improperly joins independent clauses without suitable punctuation or a conjunction: 'It was late we went home.'
questions.source: Conjunctions.pdf — F. Punctuation and Sentence Structure

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What happens when a subordinating conjunction introduces a clause?

options.A: The clause becomes dependent and normally needs an independent clause to complete the sentence
options.B: The clause becomes independent
options.C: The clause becomes a phrase
options.D: The clause becomes a question

questions.explanation: The clause becomes dependent and normally needs an independent clause to complete the sentence: 'Because he was ill' is incomplete by itself in ordinary use.
questions.source: Conjunctions.pdf — F. Punctuation and Sentence Structure

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'both...and' with parallel forms?

options.A: She likes both reading and writing.
options.B: She likes both reading and to write.
options.C: She likes both to read and writing.
options.D: She likes both reading as well as writing.

questions.explanation: Use parallel grammatical forms with both...and: 'She likes both reading and writing.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'not only...but also' with parallel forms?

options.A: She is not only intelligent but also diligent.
options.B: She is not only intelligent but diligent also.
options.C: She not only is intelligent but also diligent.
options.D: She is not only intelligent and also diligent.

questions.explanation: Keep the joined elements parallel: 'not only intelligent but also diligent.'
questions.source: Conjunctions.pdf — F. Punctuation and Sentence Structure

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'not only...but also' with verbs?

options.A: He not only sings but also dances.
options.B: He not only sings but also dancing.
options.C: He not only sing but also dances.
options.D: He not only sings and also dances.

questions.explanation: Keep the joined elements parallel: 'not only sings but also dances.'
questions.source: Conjunctions.pdf — F. Punctuation and Sentence Structure

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'both...and' with infinitives?

options.A: She wants both to study and to work.
options.B: She wants both to study and working.
options.C: She wants both studying and to work.
options.D: She wants both study and to work.

questions.explanation: Use parallel grammatical forms: 'both to study and to work.'
questions.source: Conjunctions.pdf — F. Punctuation and Sentence Structure

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'both...and' with gerunds?

options.A: She enjoys both studying and working.
options.B: She enjoys both studying and to work.
options.C: She enjoys both to study and working.
options.D: She enjoys both study and working.

questions.explanation: Use parallel grammatical forms: 'both studying and working.'
questions.source: Conjunctions.pdf — F. Punctuation and Sentence Structure

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'and' to join two phrases?

options.A: She works in the morning and in the evening.
options.B: She works in the morning or in the evening.
options.C: She works in the morning but in the evening.
options.D: She works in the morning nor in the evening.

questions.explanation: And can join two phrases: 'in the morning and in the evening.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'or' to join two words?

options.A: Ravi or Sita will lead the team.
options.B: Ravi and Sita will lead the team.
options.C: Ravi but Sita will lead the team.
options.D: Ravi nor Sita will lead the team.

questions.explanation: Or can join two words to present alternatives: 'Ravi or Sita will lead the team.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'and' to join two words?

options.A: Tea and coffee are available.
options.B: Tea or coffee are available.
options.C: Tea but coffee are available.
options.D: Tea nor coffee are available.

questions.explanation: And can join two words: 'tea and coffee.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses a conjunctive adverb with proper punctuation?

options.A: It rained; therefore, we stayed inside.
options.B: It rained, therefore, we stayed inside.
options.C: It rained therefore we stayed inside.
options.D: It rained; therefore we stayed inside.

questions.explanation: A conjunctive adverb such as therefore links ideas and usually needs appropriate punctuation: 'It rained; therefore, we stayed inside.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses a conjunctive adverb 'however'?

options.A: The task was difficult; however, she completed it.
options.B: The task was difficult, however, she completed it.
options.C: The task was difficult however she completed it.
options.D: The task was difficult; however she completed it.

questions.explanation: A conjunctive adverb such as however links ideas and usually needs appropriate punctuation: 'The task was difficult; however, she completed it.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses a conjunctive adverb 'moreover'?

options.A: The plan is costly; moreover, it is risky.
options.B: The plan is costly, moreover, it is risky.
options.C: The plan is costly moreover it is risky.
options.D: The plan is costly; moreover it is risky.

questions.explanation: A conjunctive adverb such as moreover links ideas and usually needs appropriate punctuation: 'The plan is costly; moreover, it is risky.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'because' to introduce a reason clause?

options.A: He was absent because he was ill.
options.B: He was absent because of he was ill.
options.C: He was absent because of his ill.
options.D: He was absent because ill.

questions.explanation: Because introduces a reason clause: 'He was absent because he was ill.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'since' to introduce a reason?

options.A: Since you are here, help me.
options.B: Since you are here, so help me.
options.C: Since you are here, but help me.
options.D: Since you are here, help me since.

questions.explanation: Since can introduce a reason: 'Since you are here, help me.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'as' to introduce a reason?

options.A: As it was late, we left.
options.B: As it was late, so we left.
options.C: As it was late, but we left.
options.D: As it was late, we left as.

questions.explanation: As can express reason: 'As it was late, we left.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'if' to introduce a condition?

options.A: You will pass if you work hard.
options.B: You will pass if you will work hard.
options.C: You will pass if you worked hard.
options.D: You will pass if you are working hard.

questions.explanation: If introduces a condition: 'You will pass if you work hard.' In ordinary future condition clauses, use present simple after if.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'unless' to introduce a condition?

options.A: You will not succeed unless you work hard.
options.B: You will not succeed unless you do not work hard.
options.C: You will not succeed unless you will work hard.
options.D: You will not succeed unless you worked hard.

questions.explanation: Unless means if...not: 'You will not succeed unless you work hard.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'provided that'?

options.A: You may enter provided that you have a ticket.
options.B: You may enter provided that you will have a ticket.
options.C: You may enter provided that you had a ticket.
options.D: You may enter provided that having a ticket.

questions.explanation: Provided that means only if or on the condition that: 'You may enter provided that you have a ticket.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'as long as' to mean 'on condition that'?

options.A: You can stay as long as you remain quiet.
options.B: You can stay as long as you will remain quiet.
options.C: You can stay as long as you remained quiet.
options.D: You can stay as long as you are remaining quiet.

questions.explanation: As long as can mean on condition that: 'You can stay as long as you remain quiet.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'in case'?

options.A: Take an umbrella in case it rains.
options.B: Take an umbrella in case it will rain.
options.C: Take an umbrella in case it rained.
options.D: Take an umbrella in case raining.

questions.explanation: In case introduces a precaution against a possible event: 'Take an umbrella in case it rains.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'so that' to introduce purpose?

options.A: She spoke slowly so that everyone could understand.
options.B: She spoke slowly so that everyone can understood.
options.C: She spoke slowly so that everyone could understood.
options.D: She spoke slowly so that everyone understands could.

questions.explanation: So that introduces purpose: 'She spoke slowly so that everyone could understand.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'before' to introduce an earlier time?

options.A: Wash your hands before you eat.
options.B: Wash your hands before you will eat.
options.C: Wash your hands before you ate.
options.D: Wash your hands before eating you.

questions.explanation: Before introduces an earlier time: 'Wash your hands before you eat.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'after' to introduce a later time?

options.A: We went home after the meeting ended.
options.B: We went home after the meeting will end.
options.C: We went home after the meeting ends.
options.D: We went home after ending the meeting.

questions.explanation: After introduces a later time: 'We went home after the meeting ended.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'until' to introduce a time endpoint?

options.A: Wait until I return.
options.B: Wait until I will return.
options.C: Wait until I returned.
options.D: Wait until I am returning.

questions.explanation: Until introduces the endpoint of an action or state: 'Wait until I return.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'as soon as'?

options.A: Call me as soon as you arrive.
options.B: Call me as soon as you will arrive.
options.C: Call me as soon as you arrived.
options.D: Call me as soon as arriving you.

questions.explanation: As soon as means immediately after: 'Call me as soon as you arrive.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'whenever'?

options.A: Whenever I visit, she welcomes me.
options.B: Whenever I visit, so she welcomes me.
options.C: Whenever I visit, but she welcomes me.
options.D: Whenever I visit, she welcomes me whenever.

questions.explanation: Whenever means every time that: 'Whenever I visit, she welcomes me.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'once' as a conjunction?

options.A: Once you finish, submit the paper.
options.B: Once you finish, so submit the paper.
options.C: Once you finish, but submit the paper.
options.D: Once you finish, submit the paper once.

questions.explanation: Once can mean as soon as or after: 'Once you finish, submit the paper.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'than' to introduce a comparison?

options.A: She is older than I am.
options.B: She is older as I am.
options.C: She is older that I am.
options.D: She is older when I am.

questions.explanation: Than introduces the second element of a comparison: 'She is older than I am.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'as if'?

options.A: He talks as if he knows everything.
options.B: He talks as if he knew everything so.
options.C: He talks as if he knows everything but.
options.D: He talks as if he knows everything as if.

questions.explanation: As if introduces an imagined or apparent manner: 'He talks as if he knows everything.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'as though'?

options.A: He behaved as though he knew everything.
options.B: He behaved as though he knew everything so.
options.C: He behaved as though he knew everything but.
options.D: He behaved as though he knew everything as though.

questions.explanation: As though introduces an imagined or apparent manner: 'He behaved as though he knew everything.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'because' and 'so' separately (not together)?

options.A: Because he was ill, he stayed home.
options.B: Because he was ill, so he stayed home.
options.C: He was ill, because so he stayed home.
options.D: So he was ill, because he stayed home.

questions.explanation: Do not normally combine because and so in one cause-result construction. Use either 'Because he was ill, he stayed home' or 'He was ill, so he stayed home.'
questions.source: Conjunctions.pdf — E. Important Conjunction Pairs and Usage Rules

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'although' without 'but'?

options.A: Although it rained, we played.
options.B: Although it rained, but we played.
options.C: Although it rained, so we played.
options.D: Although it rained, because we played.

questions.explanation: Do not normally combine although and but for the same contrast: 'Although it rained, we played.'
questions.source: Conjunctions.pdf — E. Important Conjunction Pairs and Usage Rules

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'despite' with a gerund?

options.A: Despite being tired, he continued.
options.B: Despite he was tired, he continued.
options.C: Despite of being tired, he continued.
options.D: Despite that he was tired, he continued.

questions.explanation: Despite is a preposition followed by a noun phrase or gerund: 'despite being tired.'
questions.source: Conjunctions.pdf — E. Important Conjunction Pairs and Usage Rules

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'during' with a noun phrase?

options.A: During the lesson, the lights went out.
options.B: During I was studying, the lights went out.
options.C: During of the lesson, the lights went out.
options.D: During I studied, the lights went out.

questions.explanation: During is a preposition followed by a noun phrase: 'During the lesson, the lights went out.'
questions.source: Conjunctions.pdf — E. Important Conjunction Pairs and Usage Rules

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'because of' with a noun phrase?

options.A: He stayed home because of his illness.
options.B: He stayed home because of he was ill.
options.C: He stayed home because of being he was ill.
options.D: He stayed home because of he was sick.

questions.explanation: Because of is a prepositional phrase followed by a noun phrase: 'because of his illness.'
questions.source: Conjunctions.pdf — E. Important Conjunction Pairs and Usage Rules

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'unless' without an extra negative?

options.A: Unless you hurry, you will miss the bus.
options.B: Unless you do not hurry, you will miss the bus.
options.C: Unless you hurry, you will not miss the bus.
options.D: Unless you will hurry, you will miss the bus.

questions.explanation: Unless generally means if...not: 'Unless you hurry, you will miss the bus' = 'If you do not hurry, you will miss the bus.'
questions.source: Conjunctions.pdf — E. Important Conjunction Pairs and Usage Rules

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'if' to introduce a condition?

options.A: If it rains, stay home.
options.B: If it rains, so stay home.
options.C: If it rains, but stay home.
options.D: If it rains, stay home if.

questions.explanation: If commonly introduces a condition: 'If it rains, stay home.'
questions.source: Conjunctions.pdf — E. Important Conjunction Pairs and Usage Rules

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'whether' to introduce alternatives?

options.A: I wonder whether he will come.
options.B: I wonder if whether he will come.
options.C: I wonder that whether he will come.
options.D: I wonder whether he will come or not so.

questions.explanation: Whether introduces alternatives or an indirect yes/no question: 'I wonder whether he will come.'
questions.source: Conjunctions.pdf — E. Important Conjunction Pairs and Usage Rules

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'till' or 'until'?

options.A: Wait here until I return.
options.B: Wait here until I will return.
options.C: Wait here until I returned.
options.D: Wait here until I am returning.

questions.explanation: Both till and until mean up to a time and are generally interchangeable: 'Wait here until I return.'
questions.source: Conjunctions.pdf — E. Important Conjunction Pairs and Usage Rules

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'while' to indicate simultaneous time?

options.A: While I was reading, the lights went out.
options.B: While the reading, the lights went out.
options.C: During I was reading, the lights went out.
options.D: While I was reading, so the lights went out.

questions.explanation: While can indicate simultaneous time and is followed by a clause: 'While I was reading, the lights went out.'
questions.source: Conjunctions.pdf — E. Important Conjunction Pairs and Usage Rules

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'so' to show a result?

options.A: It was late, so we left.
options.B: It was late, so that we left.
options.C: It was late, so we left so.
options.D: It was late, so left we.

questions.explanation: So can join clauses to show a result: 'It was late, so we left.'
questions.source: Conjunctions.pdf — E. Important Conjunction Pairs and Usage Rules

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'so that' to introduce purpose?

options.A: We left early so that we could catch the bus.
options.B: We left early so we could catch the bus so that.
options.C: We left early so that we can catching the bus.
options.D: We left early so that we could catch the bus so.

questions.explanation: So that introduces a purpose clause: 'We left early so that we could catch the bus.'
questions.source: Conjunctions.pdf — E. Important Conjunction Pairs and Usage Rules

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'both...and' with two subjects?

options.A: Both Ravi and Sita passed.
options.B: Both Ravi or Sita passed.
options.C: Both Ravi nor Sita passed.
options.D: Both Ravi as well as Sita passed.

questions.explanation: Both...and is the correct pair: 'Both Ravi and Sita passed.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'either...or' with two subjects?

options.A: You can either stay or leave.
options.B: You can either stay nor leave.
options.C: You can either stay and leave.
options.D: You can either stay but leave.

questions.explanation: Either...or indicates choice between alternatives: 'You can either stay or leave.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'neither...nor' with two subjects?

options.A: Neither Ravi nor Sita was present.
options.B: Neither Ravi or Sita was present.
options.C: Neither Ravi and Sita was present.
options.D: Neither Ravi but Sita was present.

questions.explanation: Neither...nor indicates negation of both alternatives: 'Neither Ravi nor Sita was present.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'not only...but also'?

options.A: She is not only intelligent but also hardworking.
options.B: She is not only intelligent and also hardworking.
options.C: She is not only intelligent or also hardworking.
options.D: She is not only intelligent nor also hardworking.

questions.explanation: Not only...but also indicates emphatic addition: 'She is not only intelligent but also hardworking.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'whether...or'?

options.A: I do not know whether he will come or stay.
options.B: I do not know whether he will come and stay.
options.C: I do not know that whether he will come or stay.
options.D: I do not know if whether he will come or stay.

questions.explanation: Whether...or indicates alternative or uncertainty: 'I do not know whether he will come or stay.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'as...as'?

options.A: She is as tall as her sister.
options.B: She is as tall than her sister.
options.C: She is as tall that her sister.
options.D: She is as tall so her sister.

questions.explanation: As...as indicates equality in comparison: 'She is as tall as her sister.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'so...that'?

options.A: He was so weak that he could not walk.
options.B: He was so weak so that he could not walk.
options.C: He was such weak that he could not walk.
options.D: He was so weak than he could not walk.

questions.explanation: So...that indicates degree and result: 'He was so weak that he could not walk.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'such...that'?

options.A: It was such a difficult paper that many students struggled.
options.B: It was such a difficult paper so that many students struggled.
options.C: It was so a difficult paper that many students struggled.
options.D: It was such a difficult paper than many students struggled.

questions.explanation: Such...that indicates type/degree and result: 'It was such a difficult paper that many students struggled.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'rather...than'?

options.A: I would walk rather than wait.
options.B: I would walk rather than waiting.
options.C: I would walk rather than to wait.
options.D: I would walk rather than waited.

questions.explanation: Rather...than indicates preference or contrast: 'I would walk rather than wait.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'no sooner...than'?

options.A: No sooner had he arrived than it began to rain.
options.B: No sooner he had arrived than it began to rain.
options.C: No sooner had he arrived when it began to rain.
options.D: No sooner he arrived than it began to rain.

questions.explanation: No sooner...than indicates one event immediately follows another: 'No sooner had he arrived than it began to rain.' Inversion is required when no sooner begins the clause.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'hardly...when'?

options.A: Hardly had I reached home when it began to rain.
options.B: Hardly I had reached home when it began to rain.
options.C: Hardly had I reached home than it began to rain.
options.D: Hardly I reached home when it began to rain.

questions.explanation: Hardly...when indicates immediate sequence: 'Hardly had I reached home when it began to rain.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'scarcely...when'?

options.A: Scarcely had the match begun when it started raining.
options.B: Scarcely the match had begun when it started raining.
options.C: Scarcely had the match begun than it started raining.
options.D: Scarcely the match begun when it started raining.

questions.explanation: Scarcely...when indicates immediate sequence: 'Scarcely had the match begun when it started raining.'
questions.source: Conjunctions.pdf — E. Important Conjunction Pairs and Usage Rules

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'either...or' with subject-verb agreement?

options.A: Either the teacher or the students are coming.
options.B: Either the teacher or the students is coming.
options.C: Either the teacher or the students was coming.
options.D: Either the teacher or the students were coming.

questions.explanation: With either...or, the verb commonly agrees with the nearer subject: 'Either the teacher or the students are coming.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'neither...nor' with subject-verb agreement?

options.A: Neither the manager nor the workers are ready.
options.B: Neither the manager nor the workers is ready.
options.C: Neither the manager nor the workers was ready.
options.D: Neither the manager nor the workers were ready.

questions.explanation: With neither...nor, the verb commonly agrees with the nearer subject: 'Neither the manager nor the workers are ready.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'not only...but also' with subject-verb agreement?

options.A: Not only the students but also the teacher is present.
options.B: Not only the students but also the teacher are present.
options.C: Not only the students but also the teacher were present.
options.D: Not only the students but also the teacher have been present.

questions.explanation: With not only...but also, the verb commonly agrees with the subject nearer to it: 'Not only the students but also the teacher is present.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'both...and' with subject-verb agreement?

options.A: Both Ravi and Sita are ready.
options.B: Both Ravi and Sita is ready.
options.C: Both Ravi and Sita was ready.
options.D: Both Ravi and Sita has been ready.

questions.explanation: Both...and normally takes a plural verb when it joins two subjects: 'Both Ravi and Sita are ready.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'no sooner...than' with inversion?

options.A: No sooner had the train arrived than the passengers rushed in.
options.B: No sooner the train had arrived than the passengers rushed in.
options.C: No sooner had the train arrived when the passengers rushed in.
options.D: No sooner the train arrived than the passengers rushed in.

questions.explanation: The pattern is: No sooner + had + subject + past participle + than + simple past: 'No sooner had the train arrived than the passengers rushed in.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'hardly...when' with inversion?

options.A: Hardly had she sat down when the phone rang.
options.B: Hardly she had sat down when the phone rang.
options.C: Hardly had she sat down than the phone rang.
options.D: Hardly she sat down when the phone rang.

questions.explanation: The pattern is: Hardly + had + subject + past participle + when + simple past: 'Hardly had she sat down when the phone rang.'
